summary: John Welsh opens by tracing how models became capable of tool calling around mid-2024, sparking rapid proliferation of custom endpoints across organizations. This led to integration chaos: duplicated functionality, inconsistent interfaces, and costly rewrites when porting integrations between services. At Anthropic, they recognized all endpoints were converging toward something resembling MCP—get tools, get resources, elicitation of details. Welsh distinguishes two sides of MCP: the JSON RPC message specification, which he considers the real value, and the global transport standard (streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.1, session management), which is difficult but less critical. Anthropic decided to standardize on MCP for everything involving providing model context to models, regardless of where the stream goes. The MCP Gateway provides a single connect-to-MCP call returning an MCP SDK client session, with URL-based routing, automatic credential management, centralized rate limiting, and observability. The gateway receives stored credentials and creates an authenticated SDK client by passing a bearer token to the OAuth header, then plumbs read/write streams into the internal transport. Centralizing context flow provides a critical security benefit: a single point to enforce policy against prompt injection attacks, ban malicious servers, perform content classification, and audit requests. Because messages are in standardized MCP format, hooking message processors into the stream is straightforward. Adding MCP support to new services requires only importing a package, working across multiple languages internally. Engineers focus on features, not plumbing. Welsh's takeaways: MCP is fundamentally JSON streams and piping them is a small implementation detail; organizations should standardize on something—MCP is recommended; build pits of success where the right way is the easiest way; and centralize at the correct layer to solve shared problems once, freeing engineers for more valuable work.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: John Welsh introduces himself as a software engineer with 20 years of experience building large-scale systems, currently at Anthropic focusing on tool calling, integration, and implementing MCP support for external integrations.

sections.title: Tool Calling Explosion and Integration Chaos
sections.summary: Models became capable of tool calling around mid-2024, leading to rapid proliferation of custom endpoints. This caused integration chaos with duplicated functionality, inconsistent interfaces, and costly rewrites when porting integrations between services. Anthropic recognized all endpoints were converging toward something resembling MCP.

sections.title: Two Sides of MCP and Standardization Decision
sections.summary: Welsh distinguishes the JSON RPC message specification (the real value) from the global transport standard (streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.1, session management). Anthropic decided to standardize on MCP for everything involving providing model context to models, regardless of where the stream goes.

sections.title: Why Standardize on MCP Internally
sections.summary: Reasons to standardize: not a competitive advantage to be good at plumbing integrations, single approach accelerates engineering, ecosystem demand makes MCP an industry standard with all major AI labs represented, and the protocol solves problems not yet encountered like sampling primitives for billing and token tracking.

sections.title: Converging Requirements and MCP Gateway Design
sections.summary: Anthropic faced converging requirements: external remote MCP services, proliferation of internal LLM-backed agents, and security concerns. Their solution is the MCP Gateway, shared infrastructure embodying the pit of success philosophy, providing a single connect-to-MCP call with URL-based routing, automatic credential management, rate limiting, and observability.

sections.title: Gateway Code and Transport Flexibility
sections.summary: Client libraries call connect_to_mcp with URL, org ID, and signed token, returning an MCP SDK client session. Transports are flexible: websockets internally, but gRPC, Unix sockets, or even IMAP email all work by piping read/write streams into an MCP SDK session.

sections.title: Unified Authentication and Portable Credentials
sections.summary: OAuth is handled at the gateway so consumers avoid complexity. Credentials are portable across batch jobs and services without reauthentication. Internal services don't have to manage tokens directly.

sections.title: Centralized Context, Security, and Takeaways
sections.summary: The gateway receives stored credentials and creates an authenticated SDK client by passing a bearer token to the OAuth header, then plumbs read/write streams into the internal transport. Centralizing context flow provides a single point for security policy enforcement—defense against prompt injection attacks, banning malicious servers, content classification, and auditing. Standardized MCP message formats make it easy to hook in message processors. Adding MCP support to new services is just importing a package across any language. Welsh's takeaways: MCP is fundamentally JSON streams with piping as a small implementation detail; standardize on something; build pits of success; centralize at the correct layer to solve shared problems once.
